title: LLM Unlearning with LLM Beliefs
claim: Suppressing only target outputs merely squeezes probability into related regions; adding the model's own high-confidence beliefs to the objective gives thorough forgetting.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, red dashed observation vs blue dashed algorithm flow
description: The figure has two dashed-border panels. The left panel is pink with a red border and is titled 'Observation: LLM unlearning can cause spurious unlearning'. It has a Q&A bubble about an animal that says 'meow'. After unlearning, 'Cat' is replaced by 'Kitty', and a sad robot marks this as 'Fail!'. Below the bubble is a bar chart of probability over vocabulary. The 'Cat' bar is pushed down. Mass moves up into a grey 'High-Likelihood Region' of semantically similar tokens such as Kitty and Feline. Unrelated tokens such as Tiger and Dog stay low. The label 'Squeezing effect redistributes prob.' appears beside it. The right panel is lavender with a blue border and is titled 'Algorithm: Bootstrapping framework at token (BS-T) and sequence (BS-S) levels'. A vertical flow runs from the unlearning dataset through the original LLM to the unlearned LLM. Arrows labeled BS-T and BS-S branch to a model-belief cloud. Next to it are a token probability table and soft-distribution histograms that are added to a one-hot label. Together they form a soft unlearn target, and sampled sequences form an augmented dataset. The flow ends in a safe answer and a happy robot marked 'Success!'.
caption: Motivation and overview of our work. Left: Suppressing only target responses appears effective but shifts probability mass into semantically related regions (squeezing effect), yielding spurious unlearning. Right: Our bootstrapping framework addresses this by incorporating model beliefs: BS-T suppresses high-probability tokens, while BS-S augments full high-confidence sequences, enabling more thorough forgetting.
abstract: Large language models trained on vast corpora inherently risk memorizing sensitive or harmful content, which may later resurface in their outputs. Prevailing unlearning methods generally rely on gradient ascent and its variants to lower the probability of specific target responses. However, we find that this strategy induces a critical side effect: probability mass is redistributed into high-likelihood regions, often corresponding to semantically related rephrasings of the targets. We refer to this as the squeezing effect, which explains why many methods yield merely spurious unlearning, a problem further obscured by automated metrics (e.g., ROUGE, truth ratio) that misreport actual success. To address this, we propose a bootstrapping (BS) framework that explicitly links the squeezing effect with the model's own high-confidence generations, namely its model beliefs. Since model beliefs inherently capture the very high-likelihood regions where probability mass is squeezed, incorporating them into the unlearning objective directly counters the squeezing effect. By jointly suppressing both target responses and model beliefs, BS-T (token) attenuates high-probability tokens, whereas BS-S (sequence) removes entire high-confidence generations, together achieving more thorough forgetting while preserving utility. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks with various model families confirm the effectiveness of our approach.
